# Design plan: three-checks

This plan implements the closed design brief for three-checks exactly. Where the brief fixes a form, a code, a wording, an order, or an exit status, this plan repeats that fixing as the design and adds no alternative. Where the brief leaves a mechanical detail undecided, part 7 of this plan rules it and marks whether the ruling blocks stage 13.

Stage boundaries held by this plan: this document contains no code and no tests. Stage 13 writes the tests named in part 4. Stage 14 builds the program in the sequence given in part 5.

## 1. Module map

One Python program, one file, `three_checks.py`, Python standard library only. No network access, no database access, no file read beyond the bundle file and the artifact files the bundle names, and no file write beyond the three named output paths. The program is organised as small single purpose parts inside the one file. Each part below names its seam: what it takes, what it returns, and what it never does. Parts communicate only through the shapes named in part 2. No check part reads raw bundle bytes or raw parsed JSON.

### 1.1 Constants and tables part

Takes: nothing at run time.
Returns: the fixed values every other part shares. The values are the tool name, the version string ruled in part 7, the bundle byte limit of 2000000, the artifact byte limit of 2000000, the section order of brief section 3, the closed field sets for every level of the bundle, the seven evaluated property kinds, the allowed value sets stated in brief section 3, the 19 discrepancy codes of brief section 8, the consequence table of brief section 7, the absence matrix of part 1.14, the OP-4 expected, found, and cure templates of part 7, the strength line verbatim from Appendix A, the scope paragraph verbatim from Appendix A, the usage line verbatim from Appendix B, and the report fixed lines verbatim from Appendix A.
Never does: no input, no output, no computation beyond holding the tables.

### 1.2 Argument parsing part

Takes: the process argument list, without the program name.
Returns: either a run request shape holding the four paths as supplied, the four paths resolved to absolute form, and the verifier identity string, or a usage failure shape holding one usage error text from the closed list in Appendix B. Resolved absolute form means one uniform resolution with realpath semantics, as Path.resolve provides, applied to the bundle path, every artifact path, and every output path, so symlinks and dot dot spellings through symlinked directories resolve the same way in every equality test (condition C-6).
Never does: never reads any file, never tests whether a path exists, never derives the verifier identity from any other source.
Rules it carries: exactly four positional arguments in the order BUNDLE, REPORT, RESULTS, CLOSURE, then the flag `--verifier` with exactly one value. A missing argument, an extra argument, an unknown flag, and a missing identity value each produce their own Appendix B usage text. Path collision testing on resolved absolute paths also lives here, because it needs only the paths and the artifact path list is not yet known at this point for the bundle and output collisions: bundle against each output, and each output against each other output, produce the Appendix B usage texts for an output path naming an input file and for two output paths naming one file. Every path in every such test is resolved by the one uniform realpath resolution stated above (C-6); no path is resolved by textual normalisation alone. The further collision test, an output path resolving to an artifact path, runs in phase 4 of part 3, as soon as the validated bundle has supplied the artifact paths, and it produces the same usage text before anything is written.

### 1.3 Bundle reading part (reading gates)

Takes: the bundle path as supplied and its resolved form.
Returns: either the bundle bytes exactly as read plus their SHA-256 digest, or the first reading gate failure as a single input error shape.
Never does: never decodes, never parses, never reads any other file, never reads the bundle a second time.
Rules it carries: the five reading gates of brief section 5 run here and in the strict parser part together, in the fixed order of the brief, first failure only. This part owns the first three gates: cannot read, size limit, and encoding. Reading failures in the cannot read case are caught expressly as the OSError family, including FileNotFoundError and IsADirectoryError, consistent with the error families map in part 1.4 and phase 2 of part 3. The size gate compares the measured byte count with 2000000 and its error text names both values in the Appendix B form. The encoding gate tests the raw bytes: bytes that are not valid UTF-8, and bytes carrying a byte order mark, both fail this gate.

### 1.4 Strict JSON parsing part

Takes: the bundle bytes that passed the encoding gate.
Returns: either the parsed value tree in the parsed bundle shape of part 2.1, with duplicate key information preserved as data, or one input error shape for the JSON validity gate or the top level shape gate.
Never does: never validates fields, never coerces a value, never repairs a document.
Rules it carries, from the research register: parsing uses an object pairs hook at every object level so a duplicated key is detected during parsing, recorded with its full path and a detection ordinal, and the duplicated field is not validated further. Encounter order for duplicate keys (ruling R9-1, an interpretation of the brief section 5 phrase in encounter order) is the order in which the parser detects them, which is object completion order: an inner object duplicate is detected before an outer duplicate whose second key stands earlier in the document, because the object pairs hook fires when an object closes. Duplicate errors are ordered by the detection ordinal recorded in part 2.1, never by document position of the second key. A parse constant hook rejects the NaN and Infinity tokens at the JSON validity gate by raising a plain ValueError, which is not a JSONDecodeError. The JSON validity gate therefore catches ValueError around the parse, expressly, so the catch covers both decode errors and the hook rejection (condition C-1). Surrogate gate (ruling R9-2, an interpretation of the brief section 3 sentence that a string holding an unpaired surrogate is invalid, grounded on the tier-test precedent ruling for the same sentence form): a string holding an unpaired surrogate, in a value or in a field name, at any level, including inside a discarded duplicate value, fails at the JSON validity reading gate with the Appendix B template for that gate, the bundle file is not valid JSON. No field path is printed for that failure, because it is a gate failure, first failure only, and no such string reaches field validation. Placement for R9-2 (condition C-3, changing no outcome): the surrogate scan runs inside the object pairs hook, over every key and every value as the hook receives them, with a deep walk of each value, because a discarded duplicate value is invisible to a post parse walk; a walk of the top level value covers strings standing in lists and a non object top level. A parser depth failure is caught expressly as RecursionError and reported at the JSON validity gate as invalid JSON, never as an unhandled error (condition C-4). The depth fixture for this gate is restated in part 4, group T2: its nesting form is objects, nested one object inside the next, to a depth of 10000, which fails on Python 3.12.3 on this build, and the test asserts only the error line form; the failure boundary is a property of this CPython build and its C scanner, not of the recursion limit setting alone, no failure at the same depth is assumed for a different build, and it is not a fixed brief value. Error families at this gate (condition C-10): the gate catches three separate families expressly, ValueError for decode errors and the parse constant rejection, RecursionError for depth, and OSError for reading, including FileNotFoundError and IsADirectoryError; the writing part carries the OSError family for writing, stated in part 1.21 and part 3. Time form: a time string is judged by the express form test in part 1.6 before any library parse, and no time string reaches a library parse in this part. The top level value must be an object; any other top level kind fails the top level shape gate. Numbers keep their parsed kind: an integer stays an integer, and any float, including a float produced by an overflowing exponent, stays a float and is therefore the wrong type for every integer and digest field downstream.

### 1.5 Field validation part

Takes: the parsed value tree and the duplicate key records from the strict parser part.
